action_criteria.expected_evidence: Tremor that entrains to a 3 Hz tapping rhythm and stops or lessens with distraction, with no bradykinesia or rigidity
action_criteria.label: Examine the tremor for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: Two months of bilateral hand tremor of abrupt onset with remissions: the diagnosis rests on positive signs such as entrainment and distractibility, and on the absence of parkinsonian or other neurological signs, not on the exclusion of other disease (DSM-5 criterion B).

citations: Bhatia KP et al. Consensus statement on the classification of tremors. Mov Disord 2018;33:75-87
action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal TSH, against a thyroid cause of an enhanced physiological tremor
action_criteria.label: Thyroid function (TSH)
action_criteria.rationale: Hyperthyroidism enhances physiological tremor, and a new tremor in a young adult is checked with a TSH; she has no heat intolerance, weight loss, palpitations or goiter, so the test is good practice rather than required.

citations: Bhatia KP et al. Consensus statement on the classification of tremors. Mov Disord 2018;33:75-87
action_criteria.expected_evidence: SSRI-induced tremor raised as a possible contributor, with no interacting drug
action_criteria.label: Review sertraline as a possible contributor to the tremor
action_criteria.rationale: SSRIs can cause or enhance tremor, and a drug cause is part of the assessment of any new tremor; her dose has been unchanged for 2 years, so sertraline is an unlikely sole cause, and the review decides whether a medicine change belongs in the plan.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies anxiety and post-traumatic symptoms to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment, if it will guide therapy
action_criteria.rationale: It can quantify her anxiety and the post-traumatic symptoms after the accident to target psychological treatment, but it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway, so it is justified only when the result will shape therapy.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional tremor) based on entrainment of the tremor to an imposed rhythm and its distractibility during a ballistic movement and mental arithmetic, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus), including functional tremor retraining.
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid generalized anxiety disorder and the anxiety and intrusive memories since the car accident.

avoided_actions.rationale: She has had no loss of consciousness, syncope or palpitations; an ECG answers no question about a tremor.
There is no murmur, syncope or embolic question; an echocardiogram answers nothing in this patient.
Her resting rate is 78 with no palpitations or syncope; nothing suggests an arrhythmia.
She did not hit her head in the accident and has no focal sign; a head CT adds radiation and no information.
She is afebrile with no inflammatory, encephalopathic or neuropathic feature; a lumbar puncture would add risk and change nothing.
FDG-PET has no diagnostic role in a functional tremor and answers no question in this patient.
Strength, reflexes and sensation are normal; nerve conduction studies and needle EMG examine nerve and muscle and answer no question about this tremor.
Sensation is normal in all limbs; somatosensory evoked potentials answer no question here.
There is no bradykinesia, rigidity or decrement and the tremor entrains and is distractible; there is no parkinsonism for a dopamine transporter scan to confirm or exclude.
The tremor has positive functional features and the examination has no focal, pyramidal, cerebellar or parkinsonian sign; brain imaging has no question to answer.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder — functional tremor of both arms

differential.diagnosis: Enhanced physiological tremor, including SSRI-induced tremor
differential.key_features: Sertraline can enhance physiological tremor, but the dose has been unchanged for 2 years; the abrupt onset after the accident, complete remissions, entrainment and distractibility do not fit a drug-enhanced physiological tremor.
Bilateral action tremor at about 8 Hz, but abrupt onset, complete remissions, a rest component, variable frequency, entrainment, distractibility and no family history argue against it.
No heat intolerance, weight loss, palpitations, goiter or lid lag, a resting rate of 78, and a normal TSH and free T4.
No bradykinesia, decrement, rigidity, hypomimia or reduced arm swing; the tremor was bilateral from onset and entrains to an imposed rhythm.

key_clinical_evidence: Entrainment of the right hand tremor to a 3 Hz rhythm tapped with the left hand, and its suppression during a ballistic movement and mental arithmetic, are rule-in signs of functional tremor; the variability and the coactivation sign are supportive.
There is no bradykinesia, rigidity, decrement or other neurological sign and the gait is normal, so neither parkinsonism nor a structural lesion is raised and no imaging is needed.
TSH is normal, and sertraline at a dose unchanged for 2 years is at most a contributor to the tremor.

Abrupt onset after a minor car accident, with complete remissions away from work, is typical of functional tremor and supportive context; the accident is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A mother's hypothyroidism does not make hyperthyroidism likely in her; one TSH answers the question, and it is normal.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Order thyroid antibodies, thyroid ultrasound or a nuclear scan for a thyroid cause of the tremor

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Tremor is a known SSRI effect, but a stable dose for 2 years, abrupt onset, remissions, entrainment and distractibility make sertraline at most a contributor; stopping it would remove her anxiety treatment without treating the tremor.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the tremor to sertraline and stop it, without making the positive diagnosis

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A physical or emotional trigger is common at the onset of functional tremor and is supportive context, not a substitute for the positive signs; she did not hit her head and the examination has no focal sign.
red_herrings.data_point: Low-speed rear-end car accident 2 months ago, with intrusive memories since
red_herrings.intended_effect: Make the diagnosis from the accident alone, without positive signs; or look for a head or neck injury to explain the tremor

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional tremor: entrainment to an imposed rhythm and distractibility during a ballistic movement and mental arithmetic, with supportive variability and a coactivation sign. No bradykinesia, rigidity or other neurological sign.

current_medications.summary: No clinically significant interactions among the current medicines. Tremor is a listed adverse effect of sertraline.
warnings: Sertraline: tremor is a recognized adverse effect of SSRIs, usually a fine postural and action tremor that appears after the drug is started or the dose is increased; at a stable dose it can still enhance physiological tremor.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward case: abrupt-onset bilateral hand tremor after a minor car accident, with entrainment, distractibility and no parkinsonian or other neurological sign.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: The required work-up is the examination, which finds entrainment and distractibility; a TSH and a review of sertraline are recommended. The stable SSRI, a mother with thyroid disease and the disabling severity invite attributing the tremor to the drug, a thyroid work-up beyond one TSH, or a dopamine transporter scan and brain imaging.
key_positive_signs: distractibility during ballistic movement and mental arithmetic

patient.history_present_illness: A 34-year-old right-handed elementary school teacher is admitted from the emergency department with 2 months of shaking of both hands. It began abruptly on the evening of a minor car accident, in which her stationary car was struck from behind at low speed; she was not injured and did not hit her head. The shaking was fully developed within hours, involves both hands and forearms, and is worst when she writes on the board, holds a cup or feels watched. It has stopped completely twice for several days, during a week's holiday and a weekend with her sister, and returned each time she went back to work. Over the past week it has become so severe that she can no longer write and has great difficulty feeding herself, and she came to the emergency department after spilling a hot drink over her hand. She has noticed no stiffness, slowness, falls, smaller handwriting, change in her voice or loss of smell, and no heat intolerance, palpitations, weight loss or diarrhea. She has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for 2 years for generalized anxiety disorder, at an unchanged dose, and drinks two cups of coffee a day. Since the accident she avoids driving, has intrusive memories of the impact and sleeps poorly.

neurological_exam.additional: When she taps a 3 Hz rhythm with the left hand, the right hand tremor changes to the same 3 Hz rhythm. The tremor stops while she makes a quick reach with the other hand and lessens markedly during serial 7 subtraction. When the examiner moves her wrist passively, simultaneous contraction of the flexors and extensors is felt as the tremor starts.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose accurate, with the same variable tremor and no intention component; heel-to-shin normal bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Eye movements full with normal saccades, no nystagmus. Normal facial expression and blink rate. No head, jaw or voice tremor. Remaining cranial nerves normal.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal gait with normal arm swing and turning; tandem gait normal; pull test normal.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented, anxious, cooperative. Speech fluent, normal volume and prosody. Attention and memory intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Tremor of both hands and forearms, present at rest with the arms supported, with posture and with action, at about 8 Hz but varying in frequency and amplitude from moment to moment and between positions; the amplitude increases when attention is drawn to it. Bulk and tone normal, with no rigidity, including during activation of the opposite hand. Finger taps, hand opening and foot taps are fast and full with no decrement. Strength 5/5 throughout.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in the arms and legs. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, vibration and joint position sense normal in all limbs.

physical_exam.skin: A healing superficial burn on the dorsum of the right hand; skin otherwise normal.
